extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the methods a novelist uses: how to choose and combine presentation modes (scenic vs panoramic, pictorial vs dramatic), whose voice to adopt, how to prepare scenes, and how to make the book cohere around a single subject or 'image'. Uses Flaubert's Madame Bovary as primary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and clarity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist should have one clear subject or meaning for the book; the work should not present many conflicting aspects but a single identifiable point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "Flaubert has only one word to say, and it is impossible to find more than a single meaning in it." The book should be a point in the sphere of criticism — a "motionless pole" — to which critics and readers can refer. The summary or 'argument' of events does not by itself reveal the subject; the way facts are presented determines the subject. Ensure the chosen subject is irreducible and central to every choice of treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the subject before composing
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should thoroughly know and fix the subject in mind before attempting its artistic treatment; the material should remain 'quiescent' rather than demanding new directions during composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As described: Flaubert worked 'year after year' upon his subject without finding anything to disturb or distract him; his imagined book 'never left its place by a hair’s breadth.' This avoids the novelist struggling with unforeseen demands from the material. If the subject is not mastered, the writer may face the 'double strain' of discovering new elements while trying to write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-as-image: use facts to create a single image
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel is not merely a row of facts; facts have no validity until they are used to form a single image or meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "The book is not a row of facts, it is a single image; the facts have no validity in themselves, they are nothing until they have been used." Facts are the groundwork, but the novelist's art is to make them 'tell' by arranging them into an image that conveys the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show rather than state; make truth intrinsic to the book
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel must 'look true' by virtue of its internal methods, not by asserting external attestation or simple statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts Defoe's asserted historic truthfulness with Flaubert's method: "in a novel, strictly so called, attestation of this kind is... irrelevant; the thing has to look true, and that is all." Avoid relying on external authority; instead arrange presentation so the reader perceives truth from within the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate selection of information (method of placing statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist chooses a path in how to place statements and selects which information to offer; this choice is the writer's 'method'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "by his method, by his various methods, we mean his manner of choosing his path." The difference between writers may be in how they place and order their assertions — direct narrative versus more roundabout approaches — and critics should attend to these choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic versus panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to present incidents as immediate scenes (scenic) or as broad surveys of lives and events (panoramic); these are technically distinct modes of presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and examples: scenic = presenting a particular scene/selected hour (e.g., opening scene of Bovary's arrival at school); panoramic = surveying lives from a height with a wide range of vision (e.g., summaries of background). Many novels alternate both; the critic notices how and when the author shifts from one to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (subjective) versus dramatic (objective) rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to render an occasion pictorially — bathed in a character's mood and inner perception — or dramatically — by presenting visible and audible facts that could be staged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the ball is treated pictorially in Emma’s terms, where the mood fills the foreground; the cattle-show (cornices) is more dramatic, with facts in the fore and things that might be put on stage without loss. The choice affects whether the reader watches emotion or witnesses action, and an author may mix both as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial presence and 'impersonality' as dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's opinions must appear implicitly through dramatization and embodiment rather than explicit statements; 'impersonality' is achieved by tactfully expressing feeling rather than declaring it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "The famous 'impersonality'... lies only in the greater tact with which they express their feelings — dramatizing them, embodying them in living form, instead of stating them directly." The writer still shows what he thinks by the choices he makes; avoid direct authorial didacticism when a dramatized embodiment will serve better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of voice/point-of-view: author vs character
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear when the narrative voice is the author's and when it is mediated through a character; use these shifts consciously to control interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Flaubert sometimes speaks with his own voice and sometimes 'through one of the people' (mainly Emma). When the author 'retreats' and uses Emma's eyes, landscape and incident adopt her color. Occasional brief shifts to other characters' views are permissible, but the shifts must be motivated and controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and maintain an appropriate centre of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which character's mind or which stance will 'command' the subject (the centre of vision), and avoid unnecessary, haphazard plunges into other minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "shift the point of view no more often than he need; and if the subject can be completely rendered by showing it as it appears to a single one of the figures in the book, then there is no reason to range further." In Madame Bovary the centre is Emma; occasional other centres are used sparingly for purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage alternation and fusion of methods intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may alternate scenic/panoramic, pictorial/dramatic, authorial/character voice, but such alternations must be governed by a principle tied to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "we see them alternated, united, imposed one on another... In well-fashioned work it is always interesting to discover how method tends to be laid upon method." Critics should look for the principle on which methods are mingled and varied; these mixtures form layers and stratifications in treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of plan and economy of latitude
rubrics_metrics.description: While methods may vary, the author must be consistent on some plan and allow no more latitude than required by the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "The only law that binds him throughout... is the need to be consistent on some plan, to follow the principle he has adopted; ... to allow himself no more latitude than he requires." Arbitrary or gratuitous liberties weaken the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes must be necessary, prepared, and placed for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene must be wanted by the story, prepared for by prior material, and placed where it will illuminate the subject and advance the action; unnecessary scenes are weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "A scene that is not really wanted, and that does nothing in particular — a scene that for lack of preparation fails to make its effect — is a weakness in a story." Scenes are "the articulation of the book" and should recur for climaxes and resolutions; by the time a scene is reached, "nothing is wanting to its opportunity."

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize subject/characteric impression over mere events
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis of a novel should be on the subject and the living impression of people and place rather than on the chain of incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: "None of the events really matter for their own sake; they might have happened differently... They are not in themselves what he has to say, they simply illustrate it." When recalling a book, readers remember impressions and characters more than plot steps; write so events serve that impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intervention used judiciously to supply necessary context or interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist should intervene with superior knowledge when readers need background or the inner thoughts of characters to understand an incident that cannot be perceived by mere observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "There comes a juncture at which... it is necessary for us to know more than we could have made out by simply looking and listening... the author... recalls certain circumstances... or... enters their consciousness." Use intervention only when it illuminates and is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method should arise from subject and reflect the writer's imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular combination of methods used in a book should be congenial to the subject and will reveal qualities of the novelist's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "the story that occurs to him... will be that which asks for the kind of treatment congenial to his hand; and so his method will be a part of himself, and will tell us about the quality of his imagination." Choose methods that best serve the subject rather than following fashions or saving effort.
